en: Your bullet was as large as a sheep’s head,
They bound it in battle and passed on,
They had bound him to true death,
They forced his head to the ground,
Life left him before his face had changed,
Death’s bullet struck his temple,
Our dear elder Köböy,
Had gone to single combat with no other choice.
Seeing this, Ebegey,
Parted from his comrade in sacrifice,
Called the Kyrgyz into the midst,
Broken with grief and separation,
Left diminished and alone,
His soul seared by the loss,
Left solitary like an ascetic,
Without offspring, gathering his remaining strength,
None remained standing; they died,
The figure before them,
Hero Köböy, hard as a hammer,
A warrior-khan to the Kyrgyz,
A close companion beneath one coat,
The people embraced his spreading fame,
Ebegey and Köböy had been born,
Those shared twins,
If a fated bullet struck from above,
Giving a final blessing to the lips,
The enemy could not take the dear hero,
His banner-head stood in the stormy trap,
Nothing remained for those who saw,
Now let me die for his sake.
A lion-hearted soul, truly born,
Created for true honor,
Let me surrender this fly-like life,
Saying this, Ebegey,
Mounted the pale horse of pure milk-color,
Fastening on his coat of mail,
Spurring from right and left,
Casting himself into the countless ranks,
Crying out, “Comrades in sacrifice!”
He attacked hero Ozu,
They fought face to face,
The myriad mouths opened wide,
Frowning, they showed no mercy,
Without delay they thrust their spears,
The dear spears shattered in battle,
Their bodies were wounded and bent,
All their blood was washed away,
No bullet could halt their grappling,
They struggled with all their strength,
They waged a fierce conflict,
Each one was a mighty champion,
They fought from the first blow,
They committed a harsh and savage deed,
Each set his teeth against the other,
They covered the hilltop in blood,
They turned the whole struggle into dust,
Unable to overcome one another,
Their strength mounted,
They seized collars and wrestled,
They grappled like rival hordes,
They struck without restraint,
They fought with crushing blows,
They stood locked collar to collar,
They reached the horses’ flanks,
Against mounted China, the Kyrgyz were few.
All that remained was entrusted to God,
Who took lives whenever he grappled,
Behind him came the masterful Jooshuk,
He unleashed extraordinary devastation,
Your elder, the warrior Ebegey,
A hammer is needed against hard iron,
For the final strength of the arm, God is there,
A brave youth goes against the oppressor,
Without making even one supporting figure known,
My elder, whose fortune was complete,
Would he not know this grave?
If what was told was truly so,
Hero Ebegey was a brave man,
A man whose desire was fulfilled,
A man of the Muslim people,
Would he not know our measure?
First, against the sharp-eyed Manchu foe,
Would my khan not remain safe?
Saying the foe had become needless,
If the reported rumor was true,
Would the black Chinese not mount?
With no champion and no support,
Saying Karman mounted the horse,
May God strike his house.
Would he not demand blood-price for his khan?
Ozu, frightened by this,
Used great force in the assault,
Living on in this world without dying,
He became iron-hearted.
True death had not yet reached him,
The blue-maned one who suffered humiliation,
Hero Ebegey, beware,
To a son greater than his father,
A brave man who knew how to seize his chance.
Hero Kenen took courage,
He urged on the blue stallion,
Leaving no grief upon the earth,
Kenen did not truly yield,
No regret remained in the hero.
The gray falcon struck,
He possessed complete cunning,
May poor Kenen not perish,
Among the people he had full support.
The peerless hero Jeljetpes.
That hero was his soul-companion,
Jeljetpes departed from your elder,
The one who ranged the heights was stirred,
With heroes Ebegey and Köböy,
With young Kenen behind you,
Remaining there, he became a friend,
He proclaimed the fame of every steed,
Meeting halfway, they grappled,
They licked the edge of the keen sword,
In the irreversible humiliation of battle,
Now entering the earth once,
He sat with hero Kenen,
Among the people of the world,
Chongteñir, who shattered the people,
Through the wrath of Beijing’s great khan,
With the stern, mighty hero,
We were cast out from Beijing,
Saying my forefather was not Kyrgyz,
Why did you call me Kyrgyz?
If I live to see another day,
Renowned Kenen was a khan,
He would not turn his back when watched,
Knowing the deed that had been completed,
Watching closely, he ran,
His strength failed at that place,
Seeing the shameful deed completed,
From your word to Kenen,
Saying all yielded on the road,
From Chongteñir’s wrath,
The Kyrgyz began the battle,
Do not ask about Jeljetpes,
You settled halfway beside your elder,
Thinking wisely, he began the assault,
Find the meaning of the words he spoke.
Not letting even a crow strike at his collar,
This precious life held in trust,
Not surrendering it to Chyng Tengir,
He caused fire to blaze across the open ground,
He drove them on with his words,
Let the people know what kind of man I am,
He escaped through skill,
He found a land beside Ala-Too,
He found the Kyrgyz people there,
Kenen, hard pressed, found support,
He was a hero who became the fortune of the Kyrgyz,
A warrior who donned armor bright as white fire,
Odu and Choyun Alp,
Your precious elder Zhelzhetpes,
A warrior who stood directly before them,
Of the Kyrgyz clans, by God’s decree,
A hero who knew the art of battle,
Against the armored Chinese,
As their finest, he ruled the people,
When he stood as sovereign khan,
He was called Zhelzhetpes,
An accomplished one who rose out of the dust,
Mounting the horse Kosho-Tumar,
He joined his lament with Kenen,
He had sweet words that were spoken,
Contending for the khanate in Beijing,
He had words to speak before Chyng Tengir,
Would the blue sword stand as his companion?
The inheritance of the white-kalpak people,
Lion-hearted Kenen and Zhelzhetpes,
Cut a path straight through,
The two giants could not bear to stand still,
To unleash a reckless conflict,
From the net of iron rope.
From the mouth of the black calamity,
From the infidel lord’s mouth,
From the fine glowing ember,
Ebegey seized hold,
From the hands of the two champions,
He displayed his majesty,
Stretching tall, he took his stance,
The two champions would not leave the enclosure,
They came and attacked the foe,
To the beauty radiant as the moon,
His elder, hero Ebegey,
Showed his might to the people,
Facing the great giant,
Against that giant warrior,
Before one could say this or that,
In the blink of a horse’s eye,
Before he could finish speaking,
Jeljetpes was indeed a champion,
The bullet that killed all could not pierce him,
It was a battle hard even for warriors,
His hearing was keen, his voice sharp,
He turned the enemy host to blood,
He crushed what he struck like grain,
Great hardship came from what he consumed,
Old and young were cut down,
Tribe struck against tribe,
Such a champion had greater strength than you,
He shattered the enemy he faced,
Köböy’s bay thoroughbred,
Destroyed all it encountered,
You knew his retainers,
This masterless one wept,
His firm cause was stirred,
Chongkor came out of Beijing.
He forged a point fine as a hair and hot as an ember,
Your elder, the warrior Ebegey,
How could he now be rescued?
Cladding his axe in blue steel,
Intending to keep him as plunder,
Following a thousand blood-soaked tracks,
As all the Kyrgyz were about to be broken,
And the Chinese spirit was to find rest,
The moment had drawn near,
Was about to find his stratagem here.
Jeljetpes had done it,
The famed steel spear,
Jeljetpes had thrust it.
A hero whose horse champed the bit,
Saying, “Give the cloth from your mouth,”
He offered his broad bare brow,
Saying, “Give what was hewn from the mountain,”
The blow reached him as he stood,
At the very place he struck,
Where Jeljetpes reached him,
The fist drove through to blood,
Do not ask how truly he seized him,
The spoken challenge was excessive,
He was master of the great conflict,
His vast strength was like a mountain,
Ozu was a villain who came from China,
Bringing him to the stake,
The darkened place became heaven’s threshold,
By the hand of this Chongsuu,
O Chinese man whose hand was your own,
If you are a soul without mercy,
The brave man longed for his khan,
One who bore the people’s burden,
He raised his valor to the sky,
His stratagem drove them into the earth,
None remained to surrender the treasure,
The giving of all was shattered,
They fell before his valor,
Do not ask how fiercely he thundered,
With difficulty the grave mound collapsed,
Their sword points divided them,
The myriad Chinese fled.
He carried out the deed by hire,
The twisted Chinese Chongteñir,
Stood red with blood,
